title: When the Witness Burns
premise: Jude Montrose is hired by a nervous man named Aldous Wren to prove that his sister-in-law, Vivian, will not be murdered at the family's upcoming thirtieth-anniversary dinner — a strange request, since Vivian is still alive. Jude's investigation reveals that thirty years ago the Wren family covered up a death at their first anniversary gathering, and every guest's alibi from that night was manufactured together. As Jude reconstructs the old lie through her flawless memory of documents and testimony, she realizes the client isn't trying to prevent a murder but to establish an alibi for one he intends to commit. At the anniversary dinner, Jude exposes both crimes — the decades-old killing and the murder about to happen — choosing to hand the evidence not to the police but to the one survivor whose life was destroyed by the original cover-up.
about_author: Elodie Vasquez spent nine years as a claims adjuster in coastal Louisiana before turning to fiction, where her eye for paperwork's quiet betrayals became her signature. She writes mysteries about people who remember too much and are believed too little.

chapters.title: Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Jude Montrose, POV. A stranger named Aldous Wren hires her to prove his sister-in-law won't be murdered at next month's anniversary dinner, paying triple her rate before she agrees. The absurdity hooks her professional pride; the cash hooks her caution. Emotional beat: unease disguised as curiosity as Jude accepts a case with no corpse and no crime — yet.

chapters.title: The House That Remembers
chapters.summary: Jude, POV. She visits the Wren estate under pretext of an insurance review, photographing rooms and memorizing details: a locked boathouse, a portrait turned to face the wall, Vivian's bruised wrist hidden by a sleeve. Emotional beat: creeping dread — the house is staged like a scene someone has rehearsed for thirty years.

chapters.title: Three Accidents
chapters.summary: Jude, POV, with flashback texture. We learn how Jude built her reputation solving three 'accidents' the police closed, and how each victory left her hollow — justice delivered late, always. She pulls the Wren family's history and finds a fourth name: a groundskeeper who vanished in 1995, the year of the first anniversary dinner. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into obsession.

chapters.title: Alibis, Woven
chapters.summary: Jude interviews the dinner guests individually and notices their stories overlap too perfectly — same phrasing, same gaps, like testimony rehearsed from a single script. Only the eldest son, Marcus, deviates, and only when drunk. Emotional beat: the thrill of pattern recognition curdling into fear, because whoever wove these alibis is powerful enough to keep them woven.

chapters.title: What Vivian Knows
chapters.summary: Vivian Wren, POV. Vivian privately confronts Jude, revealing she hired no one — Aldous acted alone — and confesses she married into a family that bought its innocence. She gives Jude a key to the boathouse and one sentence: 'Ask what was served the night the lake froze.' Emotional beat: two wary women recognizing each other as survivors.

chapters.title: The Boathouse
chapters.summary: Jude, POV. Inside the boathouse she finds the groundskeeper's effects — a ledger proving he was blackmailing the family over a hit-and-run they committed, and a coroner's report listing his death as accidental drowning. Her photographic memory cross-references the tide tables and proves the body was moved. Emotional beat: cold fury; the past isn't buried, it's archived.

chapters.title: A Client's Confession
chapters.summary: Aldous, POV. Cornered by Jude, Aldous admits the truth: he wasn't preventing a murder but constructing one — Vivian discovered the ledger and planned to go public, so he framed her as victim-to-be while arranging her death to look like the family's enemies striking back. He offers Jude a share. Emotional beat: revulsion and temptation in equal measure; the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: Thirty Years to the Glass
chapters.summary: Jude, POV. The police won't act on a murder that hasn't happened, and Aldous accelerates the timeline. Jude realizes the dinner is both weapon and stage — and that Marcus's drunken deviation means he witnessed the original killing as a child. She must turn him before the toast. Emotional beat: racing-clock tension, isolation, the weight of being the only witness who can't forget.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Dinner
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. At the dinner, glasses rise; Jude publicly reconstructs both nights using the guests' own rehearsed words against them, while Marcus breaks and corroborates. Aldous moves on Vivian; Jude's pre-positioned recording captures the confession. Emotional beat: climax — the elegant violence of truth spoken aloud in the room built to bury it.

chapters.title: Justice, Unofficial
chapters.summary: Jude, POV. Aldous is arrested, but the original hit-and-run falls outside prosecution — statute expired, witnesses complicit. Jude gives the ledger to the groundskeeper's daughter instead of the state, letting her choose restitution. Vivian leaves the family and its money behind. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution — the law failed twice, but memory, wielded carefully, did not.
